prompt: Why do modern language models use subword tokens rather than whole words?
options: Whole words cannot be represented as integers
A word vocabulary must be huge and still produces unknown words, while subwords cover any word with a manageable vocabulary
Subwords make the model faster because attention is linear in the vocabulary
Words are not allowed to contain spaces
explanation: Word-level vocabularies need an entry for every word form (names, typos, compounds) and map everything else to an unknown token. Subword vocabularies keep common words whole and spell rare ones from pieces.

prompt: In byte-pair encoding, which pair is merged at each step?
options: The pair of tokens with the longest combined spelling
A random adjacent pair
The most frequent adjacent pair in the current corpus
The rarest adjacent pair, to keep the vocabulary diverse
explanation: Merging a pair that occurs c times (non-overlapping) shortens the corpus by exactly c tokens, so the greedy compression choice is the most frequent pair.

prompt: A corpus currently has 1000 tokens and the most frequent adjacent pair occurs 60 times (non-overlapping). After merging that pair, how many tokens does the corpus have?
explanation: Each occurrence replaces two tokens by one, so the length drops by 60: $1000-60=940$.

prompt: When encoding new text with a trained BPE tokeniser, in which order are the merge rules applied?
options: Most frequent in the new text first
In the order they were learned during training
Longest resulting token first
Alphabetical order of the pair
explanation: Later rules may be built from tokens created by earlier rules (token 258 can use token 256), so the rules must be replayed in the order they were learned, lowest rule number first.

options: Every possible input can be encoded without an unknown token, because all 256 byte values are in the base vocabulary
Every word becomes exactly one token
The tokeniser never changes the length of the text
The model understands every language equally well
explanation: Any string is a byte sequence and every byte is a token, so there is always a lossless encoding. It says nothing about efficiency or model quality in a language.

prompt: A model has width $d=1000$ and vocabulary $V=50000$. How many parameters does the input embedding table alone contain (in millions)?
explanation: The embedding table has shape $(V,d)$, so $50000\times1000=5\times10^7$ parameters, i.e. 50 million.

prompt: Why are special tokens such as end-of-text matched before the BPE merges run?
options: Because BPE is slow on long strings
So that they keep a fixed id and are never split or merged with neighbouring text
Because they are not valid UTF-8
Because special tokens are the first 256 ids
explanation: A special token is a structural marker with a reserved id. If BPE processed its characters it could be split into ordinary pieces or merged into a larger token, and the model would lose the marker.

prompt: Doubling the vocabulary of a tokeniser mainly gives which pair of consequences?
options: Shorter sequences for the same text, but a larger embedding/output table with more rarely-seen tokens
Longer sequences but fewer parameters
No change in sequence length but better spelling
Lower attention cost because the context window shrinks
explanation: More merges compress text into fewer tokens (cheaper attention, more text per context) but the embedding and output matrices grow, and the new tokens are rare and hence poorly trained.
